title: How to Plan a Year in Curriculum
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles offers a simple annual cycle for heads of department and school leaders who want curriculum improvement to survive the tyranny of the urgent. He starts from barriers: constant interruptions, and whole-school CPD that wins over only a fifth of staff. His answer is to tie CPD to the curriculum and to give each of six building blocks (assessment, learning walks, books, homework, student voice, curriculum content) a fortnight of focus in a 13-week block, with the thirteenth week for review. He explains why the sequence matters and what must be kept out of line management meetings. The argument is that a calendared, narrow, self-improving system beats a crowded agenda.
points: Whole-school CPD rarely works, so improvement should be delivered at department level and embedded in curriculum resources.
The year is divided into three 13-week blocks, each fortnight carrying one fixed focus that becomes the main line-management agenda item.
The order matters: assessment first, learning walks early before they are crowded out, then books, homework and student voice before reviewing content.
Urgent operational problems such as staffing, behaviour and attendance should be handled outside the line management meeting.
Putting every focus on the calendar at the start of the year protects the plan from competing agendas.
quotes: As soon as CPD is delivered at department level, for that subject and that team, it becomes wholly relevant. If the team also help design it, there is a much greater chance of 100% opt in.
It needs to be simple. It must focus on only those 8 things. It has to be a self improving system.
Every head of department is being stretched in multiple ways, with competing demands. It is much easier not to look in the mirror every fortnight to see how their team is actually doing.
Deal with all that stuff before or after school. NOT in your line management meetings.
Keep everything as simple as possible, because no one hears exactly what you intend to communicate. And, because you are a teacher, you talk too much.
